Most work right now is essentially rate limited by our ability to process and work with information. Moving data between systems. Reviewing a document. Looking through code for security issues. Processing log data to look for even patterns. Looking up information about a prospective client. Almost all of knowledge work is constrained by these steps, and AI has become a huge unlock to that. 

So our first step was to use AI to do these individual tasks much faster for us. That was the chatbot phenomenon that we have been experiencing for the past 3+ years. But we can still then only augment the work that we remain in the loop for, and we’re highly limited by our ability to parallelize this work by our own bandwidth and context.

But where we’re going is quite different. As AI models continue to improve at incredible rates, we can hand off more and more work to the agent. First it’s letting the agent run with a harder problem. Then it’s giving a few agents multiple parts of a task at once. But we’re not far off from being able to throw an arbitrary number of agents at a problem and just say “come back when you’ve accomplished this goal”.

A month ago, nobody had heard of JEV. Then he blanched, hit a nerve in the AI world, and quickly became the most copied model in AI. JEV is both fascinating and perplexing. It's a new kind of model and is clearly a big deal, yet even some AI insiders struggle to explain what it is while others dismiss it as just a classifier. Speaker 2 | 00:53 - 01:07 So we went to the source and asked Diogo to walk us through JEV in plain English. What it is, where it's going, and why copycats are missing the point. Talked to somebody about a million users a day, a trillion tokens a day, a third of the Fortune five hundred. Speaker 1 | 01:50 - 02:13 Where do I start? I will say that a lot of those stats don't really matter for what I feel like is the devolution. To me, I knew it would be happening when builders started playing with it and doing the weird stuff. And especially when people were starting to make apps that they maybe could have done before but didn't bother with because AI was so expensive. You know? Speaker 1 | 02:13 - 02:42 I I... We push the boundaries of intelligence per second, but I think the future is going to be intelligence per dollar primarily. This is going to further accelerate AI diffusion because enterprises will be able to mix and match frontier performance for orchestration and high end tasks, while being able to have low cost and tailored post trained models for repeatable workflows. 

Overall this dramatically increases token consumption and workloads across the stack. Great to see Meta doing this.", "createdAt": "2026-10-15T17:36:55.000Z", "url": "https://x.com/levie/status/2110787013809222141", "likes": 532, "retweets": 40, "replies": 55, "isQuote": true, "quotedTweetId": "2110778736434184611"}, {"id": "2110622982762803449", "text": "Moving from chatting back and forth with agents, to having agents that you spin up in the background to do useful work for you is probably on the order of 100X or 1000X more token consumption than what we’re seeing today. 

Most work right now is essentially rate limited by our ability to process and work with information. Moving data between systems. Reviewing a document. Looking through code for security issues. Processing log data to look for even patterns. Looking up information about a prospective client. Almost all of knowledge work is constrained by these steps, and AI has become a huge unlock to that. 

So our first step was to use AI to do these individual tasks much faster for us. That was the chatbot phenomenon that we have been experiencing for the past 3+ years. But we can still then only augment the work that we remain in the loop for, and we’re highly limited by our ability to parallelize this work by our own bandwidth and context.

But where we’re going is quite different. As AI models continue to improve at incredible rates, we can hand off more and more work to the agent. First it’s letting the agent run with a harder problem. Then it’s giving a few agents multiple parts of a task at once. But we’re not far off from being able to throw an arbitrary number of agents at a problem and just say “come back when you’ve accomplished this goal”.

We could have had AGI last year, and I still believe that to be true. Pre training is a giant dumpster fire of wasting resources. Speaker 1 | 00:18 - 00:31 When I first started this project, I literally thought it would take a week. You can now express things that you couldn't express in software before. I think that the future will be unbelievably sci fi. We're building fraud, not god. Absolutely. Speaker 2 | 00:31 - 00:53 That is Jogo Almeida, CEO of TypeSafe, the company behind JEV. A month ago, nobody had heard of JEV. Then he blanched, hit a nerve in the AI world, and quickly became the most copied model in AI. JEV is both fascinating and perplexing. It's a new kind of model and is clearly a big deal, yet even some AI insiders struggle to explain what it is while others dismiss it as just a classifier. Speaker 2 | 00:53 - 01:07 So we went to the source and asked Diogo to walk us through JEV in plain English. What it is, where it's going, and why copycats are missing the point. I'm Matt Turk, and this is the BAT Podcast. Diogo, welcome. Speaker 1 | 01:07 - 01:08 Thank you. Thank you. Hey. Speaker 2 | 01:08 - 01:38 Alright. This is a super fun time, to be doing this conversation, in part because, just yesterday, I believe, as we were recording this, you guys announced, your gigantic series a, 870,000,000 series a at a 7,500,000,000 valuation. It's been a wild three weeks just looking at some stats. Your launch video had 40,000,000 views. Talked to somebody about a million users a day, a trillion tokens a day, a third of the Fortune five hundred. Speaker 2 | 01:40 - 01:50 So, it it sounds like you're indeed building, what you call the Jivolution. I love the term. I'm just curious what it feels like from the inside. Speaker 1 | 01:50 - 02:13 Where do I start? I will say that a lot of those stats don't really matter for what I feel like is the devolution. To me, I knew it would be happening when builders started playing with it and doing the weird stuff. And especially when people were starting to make apps that they maybe could have done before but didn't bother with because AI was so expensive. You know? Speaker 1 | 02:13 - 02:42 I I... We push the boundaries of intelligence per second, but I think the future is going to be intelligence per dollar primarily. And I think really getting people to play with, like like, the idea that intelligence per dollar has dropped to orders of magnitude is what will make the Jevolution unstoppable independent of enterprise adoption, users, stats, whatever. To me, it's about people playing around with things and starting to... I can't think of a non corny way to say it, but, like, build the future. Speaker 1 | 02:43 - 03:01 You know?
